extracted.intended_audience: patent applicants, patent attorneys/agents, and patent drafters preparing USPTO abstracts
extracted.subtask_description: Drafting the patent 'Abstract of the Disclosure' to comply with 37 CFR 1.72 and MPEP 608.01(b): concise word-length, physical/format requirements, required and prohibited content, and best-practice guidance for examiner/search use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abstract word length (50–150 words; single paragraph)
rubrics_metrics.description: The abstract should be as concise as the disclosure permits, preferably 50 to 150 words. The abstract can have no more than 150 words and should be no longer than a single paragraph.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Abstracts fewer than 50 words or greater than 150 words risk rejection; aim for the preferred 50–150 range. Keep the entire abstract to a single paragraph (see physical format). Write succinctly — include essential technical content but avoid verbosity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abstract physical format (narrative, separate sheet, heading)
rubrics_metrics.description: The abstract must be in narrative form, generally limited to a single paragraph on a separate sheet and must commence on a separate sheet. Heading: 'Abstract' or 'Abstract of the Disclosure'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Place the abstract on its own page (commence on a separate sheet) and preferably follow the claims. Use the heading exactly as directed to conform with filing/printing expectations. Narrative form means prose (not claim-style bulleting).

rubrics_metrics.name: Describe disclosure sufficiently to inform reader's need to consult full patent
rubrics_metrics.description: The abstract should describe the disclosure sufficiently to assist readers in deciding whether there is a need to consult the full patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus on conveying enough technical substance so searchers/examiners/the public can determine relevance; emphasize searchable technical terms and main inventive concepts rather than marketing or speculative statements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibited content and phrasing (no merits/speculation/title repetition/stock phrases/claim-style language)
rubrics_metrics.description: Do NOT contain statements on the alleged merits or value of the claimed invention; NOT contain statements on speculative application; NOT repeat information given in the title; NOT use phrases that can be implied ('The disclosure concerns,' 'This invention relates to'); NOT use claim-style phraseology like 'means' and 'said'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid promotional language, speculation about applications, redundant title text, boilerplate lead-ins, and claim terminology. Using claim terms like 'means' or 'said' risks turning the abstract into claim recitation; instead use plain technical terms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Required content elements (what to include)
rubrics_metrics.description: A good abstract should include: a statement of what the invention is (technical area); the technical features of the invention; the principal use of the invention; a short summary of the technical disclosure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure the abstract states the field/technical area in opening words, summarizes the principal technical features and principal use, and provides a brief summary of the technical disclosure sufficient for search/classification purposes without claim formalities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rejection triggers (common rejection risks)
rubrics_metrics.description: The abstract will be rejected if: it is not on its own separate page; it is fewer than 50 words; it is greater than 150 words; contains 'alleged merits' language; uses prohibited phrases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When preparing the abstract, check: page placement, exact word count, absence of promotional/speculative wording, and avoidance of prohibited/bogus phrasing. Corrections may be required if any trigger is present.

rubrics_metrics.name: Best-practice drafting techniques
rubrics_metrics.description: Write the abstract last, after claims are finalized; mirror the broadest independent claim language (without claim formality); use clear technical terms searchable by examiners and the public; include the field of technology in opening words; avoid trademark designations and trade names.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Draft the abstract after claims to ensure it reflects claim scope; echo the broadest independent claim's concepts but in narrative form (not in claim syntax). Prefer generic technical terminology (avoid trade names/trademarks) to improve searchability and classification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intended function and users of the abstract
rubrics_metrics.description: The abstract is used by patent searchers and examiners, the public to evaluate technical disclosure, classification authorities, and database indexers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep the abstract focused on functions useful to these users: concise technical content, searchable terms, and classification-relevant features. This purpose explains why strict length/format/content rules exist.
